analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top tax rate on long-term capital gains to 15 percent for individuals and corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut the top capital gains tax rate from 28 percent to 15 percent died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Bill Archer proposed cutting the top federal tax rate on long-term capital gains from 28 percent to 15 percent for individuals, from 34 percent to 15 percent for corporations, and from 20 percent to 15 percent under the alternative minimum tax [S2][S3]. Capital gains are the profits from selling stocks, businesses, and property, and they flow overwhelmingly to the highest-income households. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1991 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large unrealized gains — mostly the wealthiest Americans, who own most stocks and business assets — would pay up to 13 percentage points less tax on profits from selling them [S2]. Corporations selling appreciated assets would get the same 15 percent ceiling [S2]. Lower rates also reward holding assets longer and realizing gains in good years.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the maximum long-term capital gains rate for individual taxpayers from 28 percent to 15 percent.
Cuts the maximum capital gains rate for corporations from 34 percent to 15 percent.
Cuts the capital gains rate under the alternative minimum tax from 20 percent to 15 percent, so even taxpayers subject to the minimum tax would pay the lower rate on gains.
Applies to taxable years ending after enactment, with transitional rules for gains realized during the year of passage.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the revenue loss, which means either higher taxes on other income, more borrowing, or smaller public services. The benefit is concentrated at the top because capital gains are reported mainly by high-income households, so the broader public effectively subsidizes a cut that mostly helps the wealthiest investors.

drawbacks.text: The revenue cost falls on everyone else: every dollar of forgone capital gains tax must be made up through other taxes, borrowing, or spending cuts.

The benefit is concentrated at the top of the income scale because capital gains income accrues overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households, so the cut functions as a large tax reduction for them rather than a broad one.

A much lower rate on gains than on wages and salaries widens the gap between how work and investment are taxed, creating an incentive to structure income as capital gains rather than ordinary compensation.
An honest supporter would acknowledge that the promised payoff — more investment and more realizations of locked-in gains — is uncertain, while the revenue cost is immediate and certain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The certain, immediate effect is a large tax cut whose benefits are concentrated among the wealthiest households and corporations, paid for by the Treasury and by other taxpayers. The hoped-for gains in investment and entrepreneurship are speculative and were never tested here, since the bill never advanced far enough to be debated on the evidence. On balance, the costs outweigh the benefits for the general public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a markup or sent it to the floor, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Representative Bill Archer introduced the bill on March 23, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law.

The bill would have cut the top capital gains rate from 28 percent to 15 percent for individuals and from 34 percent to 15 percent for corporations, and lowered the minimum-tax rate on gains to 15 percent.
It drew 20 cosponsors — 17 House Republicans and 3 House Democrats — but no further action was ever taken on it.
The Ways and Means Committee never reported the bill, and the record shows no markup, no floor vote, and no further entries after the referral before the 101st Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers and the Treasury came out ahead: the revenue that a 15 percent capital gains rate would have shifted to the wealthiest investors stayed with the public. Because the bill died quietly in committee, its supporters lost nothing more than an unpassed proposal.

for.name: Rep. Bill Archer
for.role: House Ways and Means Committee member (later its ranking Republican)
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to cut the top capital gains rate to 15 percent for individuals and corporations.

for.name: George H.W. Bush administration
for.what_they_did: The administration favored a lower capital gains rate in this period, lending weight to Republican tax-cut proposals like this one.

against.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or floor vote; the record shows no committee action after the referral, and the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were House members — 17 of 175 Republicans and 3 of 257 Democrats — and the Democratic committee chairman never advanced it, so support leaned Republican with a small Democratic tail.

industries.note: Capital gains are earned mainly by the wealthiest households, so a 15 percent ceiling would deliver most of its benefit to them, funded by revenue everyone else relies on. Their gain in this bill runs directly against the public's interest in a broad, stable tax base.

industries.industry: Wall Street, private equity, and venture capital
industries.note: A lower gains rate raises after-tax returns on buying and selling companies and assets, and encourages holding assets until the favorable rate applies. The cost is borne by the Treasury, not the industry.

The bill cuts the corporate capital gains rate from 34 percent to 15 percent, reducing tax on profits from selling land, buildings, and subsidiaries. The forgone revenue comes from the general taxpayer.
